extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in psychology of humor / popular-science readers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes LaughLab's online experiment and general principles for what makes jokes funny — including the rating method, large-scale crowdsourcing, and psychological mechanisms (superiority, relief, incongruity). Useful for understanding how to evaluate or craft jokes for broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giggleometer five-point rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rated jokes using the 'Giggleometer', a five-point scale ranging from 'not very funny' to 'very funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab asked people to rate five randomly selected jokes on this scale; these scores were used to identify top jokes. The scale is ordinal and intended to capture perceived funniness from low to high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourced submission with random sampling of ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: People from around the world were asked to submit their favorite jokes and then rate five randomly selected jokes from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab collected over 40,000 jokes and ~2 million ratings from 70 countries. Random assignment of which jokes each rater saw was used to produce aggregate rankings — implying that broad, diverse sampling and random presentation are important for robust evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / cross‑demographic appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that 'work among men and women, old and young, and across different countries' are especially notable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiseman highlighted the winning joke's universal appeal as a reason for its success — suggesting that jokes that transcend age, gender, and national boundaries score well in large, diverse samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor mechanisms: superiority, relief, and incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are often funny because they make us feel superior to others, reduce the emotional impact of anxiety-provoking situations (relief), or surprise us via incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiseman explained these three mechanisms explicitly and noted the winning hunters joke contains all three elements (feeling superior to the 'stupid' hunter, reducing anxiety about mortality, and the incongruous misunderstanding). When evaluating or crafting jokes, check for one or more of these mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural / regional variation in sense of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Results indicate fundamental differences in what people from different parts of the world find funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab presented top jokes by country (Canada, UK, Australia, USA, Belgium, Germany) showing varied styles — from wry anecdote to dark punchlines to wordplay. Understanding cultural background is vital for effective communication and for predicting how a joke will be received across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edginess / dark humor and acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many top jokes were 'uncomfortably dark'; edginess is a feature that can make jokes highly rated in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of dark or potentially offensive content can increase perceived funniness for some audiences but may limit universality. Evaluate edginess relative to audience norms and cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / provenance of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Some highly rated jokes may be adaptations or derived from older material (e.g., the winning joke was later found to be based on a 1951 Spike Milligan sketch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or curating jokes, consider whether material is original or recycled — provenance can affect attribution, perceived novelty, and ethical considerations even if it still scores as funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional / therapeutic function (mood improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can function to cheer people up or help them reframe worries (e.g., reminding people 'someone is doing something more stupid than themselves').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond eliciting laughter, consider whether a joke provides relief, perspective, or mood improvement; these emotional effects can contribute to why people value and rate certain jokes highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and availability of data for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: LaughLab made over 1000 submitted jokes publicly available online and published results in a book (Quirkology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scientific or editorial evaluation of humor, public availability of submissions and documentation (methodology, aggregate ratings) supports reproducibility and further analysis of what makes jokes work.
